Let \(R=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}]\) with norm

\[
N(a+b\sqrt{-2})=a^2+2b^2.
\]

We want a generator of

\[
I=(3,\;2-2\sqrt{-2}).
\]

Apply the Euclidean algorithm. Divide \(2-2\sqrt{-2}\) by \(3\):

\[
2-2\sqrt{-2}=3(1-\sqrt{-2})+(-1+\sqrt{-2}),
\]

and

\[
N(-1+\sqrt{-2})=1+2=3<N(3)=9.
\]

Now divide \(3\) by \(-1+\sqrt{-2}\):

\[
3=(-1+\sqrt{-2})(-1-\sqrt{-2}),
\]

so the remainder is \(0\). Hence a greatest common divisor is

\[
-1+\sqrt{-2}.
\]

Multiplying by the unit \(-1\), an equivalent generator is

\[
1-\sqrt{-2}.
\]

Indeed,

\[
3=(1-\sqrt{-2})(1+\sqrt{-2}),
\qquad
2-2\sqrt{-2}=2(1-\sqrt{-2}),
\]

so both generators lie in \((1-\sqrt{-2})\). Conversely,

\[
1-\sqrt{-2}=3(1-\sqrt{-2})-(2-2\sqrt{-2}),
\]

so \(1-\sqrt{-2}\in I\). Therefore

\[
I=(1-\sqrt{-2}).
\]

The units in \(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}]\) are only \(\pm 1\), so the generators are \(\pm(1-\sqrt{-2})\). Their norm is

\[
N(1-\sqrt{-2})=1^2+2(-1)^2=3.
\]

Moreover, any nonzero element of \(I\) has the form \((1-\sqrt{-2})\gamma\), so its norm is \(3N(\gamma)\ge 3\). Thus this is the minimal possible nonzero norm.

\[
\boxed{1-\sqrt{-2}}
\]
